newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire talks blocked on venue, report of new advance.
newsitem.headline: Zaire talks blocked on venue, report of new advance.

text.p: Efforts to end Zaire's conflict peacefully hit impasse on Wednesday over the venue of direct peace talks and an announcement of a rebel advance on the capital Kinshasa.

A senior official of the rebel alliance told a news conference in Lubumbashi on Wednesday that rebel forces have captured the towns of Ilebo, Tshikapa and Dowete, east of Kinshasa, and and are closing in on the last redoubt of President Mobutu Sese Seko's regime.

Rebel "justice minister" Mwenge Kongolo said he believed the fall of Kinshasa was a "matter of days rather than weeks" and added that in his personal opinion there would not be a bloody battle for the capital.
South Africa's efforts to stage a meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila to prevent civil war reaching the Zaire capital appeared threatened by lack of agreement on a neutral venue.

In the rebel-held territory of the Central African nation, Zairean villagers said Tutsi-dominated rebels slaughtered many Rwandan Hutu refugees at camps south of Kisangani and aid workers said they had reports up to 55,000 refugees had fled.
Kabila dismissed the reports as "total nonsense".
Rebels have seized half of Zaire's vast territory since October and are advancing on Kinshasa, the last stronghold of Mobutu's collapsing army and home to five million inhabitants.
President Mobutu's son and spokesman, Nzanga Mobutu, said on Wednesday that his father was is still prepared to meet Kabila but the question remained where.

The president, citing health reasons, wants the talks held in the Congolese capital Brazzaville across the river from Kinshasa while Kabila has proposed the rebel-held town of Lubumbashi, Nzanga told a news conference.
Nzanga said Mobutu declined on health grounds an invitation from Mandela to travel to South Africa for the talks.

Kabila, in turn, had rejected Brazzaville as an alternative venue and had instead proposed Lubumbashi. Mandela conveyed Kabila's proposal to Mobutu in a telephone conversation on Tuesday night, Nzanga said.
"President Mobutu is still agreed to the principle of talks. It's only a question of the venue," he said.
He said Mobutu, who had prostate cancer surgery last August, was not sick but still convalescing.

Asked if Mobutu would go to Lubumbashi, he replied: "That is what Kabila proposed to Mandela. In a few days time, we will know more." But pressed on whether the choice of Lubumbashi was provocative, he replied:
"Provocative, no, but this is not a neutral zone. South Africa is a neutral zone, Congo is a neutral zone, Lubumbashi is not. As you know, it is an occupied zone."
Kabila and his forces say Zaire's teeming capital Kinshasa is their final major target. Nzanga Mobutu played down rebel talk of an early attack on the city.
"He's always talking," he said of Kabila, but he added: "We cannot allow bloodshed in Kinshasa."

Diplomats said the Zaireans were already sending out feelers for an alternative venue, possibly in West Africa. Zaire's Foreign Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda last week visited Togo, which staged an African meeting on Zaire last month.
Elsewhere in Zaire, the focus fell back on the continuing plight of Rwandan Hutu refugees after Zairean villagers alleged rebels slaughtered many of them.
The villagers, travelling towards Kisangani, said a battle between rebels and refugees accompanied Tuesday's slaughter at camps near Kasese village, just south of Kisangani.
"The (rebel) army went to the camp at 8 a.m. yesterday. They killed many, many refugees -- hundreds. There was lots of shooting all morning," Alphonse Soku, a farmer, told Reuters.
"They used a mechanical digger to bury the bodies."
Two Zairean women standing nearby agreed with Soku's account. All three appeared very frightened and reluctant to talk and there was no immediate rebel reaction to the reports.
The camps at Kasese for 55,000 Rwandan refugees have been sealed off from aid workers and journalists for three days.
But Kabila told Reuters by telephone from Lubumbashi that the reports were "total nonsense" and Rwandan Hutu militiamen had attacked villagers and his rebels only intervened to stop the fighting.
"There is no truth whatsoever in these reports. The truth is that local Zaireans were attacked by the Rwandan Hutu militia and our army only stepped in to stop the fighting," he said.
